reason: The sources provide sufficient details for a surprising 45-second story with well over 10 multi-source claims about Gliese 710.
story: In about 1.29 million years, an orange dwarf star named Gliese 710 is projected to plow directly into the outer edges of our solar system's Oort cloud. Currently sitting 62 light-years away in the constellation Serpens, precision data from the Gaia spacecraft reveals this star is heading almost straight toward us at roughly 14.5 kilometers per second. At its closest approach of about 10,520 astronomical units, it will become the brightest object in our night sky besides the Sun, Moon, and Venus, shining with a magnitude of negative 2.7. While the major planets will remain safe and largely undisturbed, its immense gravity will dislodge millions of icy comets, sending a relentless shower of roughly ten naked-eye comets per year streaming into the inner solar system for millions of years.
angle: An orange dwarf star is on a direct collision course to punch straight through our solar system's comet reservoir, becoming brighter than Sirius in our night sky.

claims.claim: Gliese 710 is located in the constellation Serpens.
Gliese 710 is projected to pass near the Sun in about 1.29 million years.
The predicted minimum distance of Gliese 710 is approximately 0.051 parsecs or 10,520 astronomical units.
At its closest approach, Gliese 710 will reach an apparent visual magnitude of about -2.7.
Gliese 710 has a stellar mass of about 57% of the Sun's mass and 58% of its radius.
As of 2020, no planets have been detected orbiting Gliese 710.
Gliese 710 is currently at a distance of about 62.3 light-years from Earth.
Gliese 710 has a radial velocity approaching the Solar System at roughly 14.5 km/s.
The encounter will be the strongest disrupting encounter in the future and history of the Solar System.
The passage will trigger visibility of about ten naked-eye comets per year.
The flyby will not affect the orbits of Earth or the major planets.
The star's proper motion will peak around one arcminute per year.

disputed: The exact closest approach distance and precise timing vary slightly between calculations (e.g., Bobylev et al., Berski and Dybczyński, and Gaia DR3 updates ranging from 0.051 pc to 0.062 pc); scripts should attribute specific numbers to recent Gaia data calculations.
